prompt: `a` is a `[3]int` and `b` is a `[4]int`. Why is `a = b` refused?
hint: What does `%T` print for an array?

choices.text: Because `a` would have to grow, which takes `append`
choices.why: Arrays never grow, with `append` or anything else; the assignment fails on the types.

choices.text: The length is part of an array's type, so `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different types
choices.why: Right. `[3]int` and `[4]int` are as different as `int` and `string`.

choices.text: Because the fourth element of `b` would be lost
choices.why: The compiler does not weigh what would be lost; `[2]int` into `[3]int` is refused just the same.

choices.text: Because arrays cannot be assigned at all, only copied element by element
choices.why: `b := a` worked in section 01 and copied the whole array; the lengths are what differ here.

prompt: `a := [3]int{1, 2, 3}`, then `b := a` and `b[0] = 99`. What does `fmt.Println(a)` print?
hint: What did `b := a` make?

choices.text: `[99 2 3]`, because `a` and `b` are two names for one array
choices.why: That is how two slices of one array behave. Assigning an array copies it.

choices.text: `[1 2 3]`, because `b` is a copy of every element
choices.why: Right. `b` is a second array, so changing it leaves `a` alone.
An assignment to `b[0]` writes one element, of `b`, and nothing else.

choices.text: A compile error
choices.why: An array can be copied with `:=`, and that is exactly what happened here.

prompt: `func zero(a [3]int) { a[0] = 0 }` is called as `zero(a)` with `a` holding `[1 2 3]`. What does `a` hold afterwards?
hint: The function received something. What?

choices.text: `[1 2 3]`, because the function changed its own copy
choices.why: Right. Passing an array copies every element into the parameter.

choices.text: `[0 2 3]`, because a function changes what it is given
choices.why: With a slice it would. An array arrives as a copy.
`a[0] = 0` sets one element, and of the copy at that.

choices.text: The call is refused, since arrays are not allowed as parameters
choices.why: `zero` compiled and ran in section 01; arrays are ordinary parameters.

prompt: `n := 4` followed by `var c [n]int` is refused with `invalid array length n`, because an array's length has to be a ___.
hint: Something the compiler knows before the program runs.

prompt: Which of these are true of Go arrays? Choose all that apply.
hint: Section 01 printed each of them.

choices.text: Two arrays of the same type can be compared with `==`
choices.why: Yes: element by element, and `a == [3]int{1, 2, 3}` printed `true`.

choices.text: `append` makes an array one element longer
choices.why: An array's length is in its type and never changes; `append` works on slices.

choices.text: A constant index past the end is a compile error
choices.why: Yes: `a[3]` on a `[3]int` was refused with `index 3 out of bounds [0:3]`.

choices.text: Passing one to a function lets the function change the caller's elements
choices.why: The function receives a copy; `zero(a)` left `a` as it was.

prompt: `func sum(a [3]int) int` adds three numbers, and you have `s := []int{1, 2, 3}`. What does `sum(s)` do?
hint: Compare the two types as `%T` would print them.

choices.text: It returns 6, since `s` has exactly three elements
choices.why: The length of `s` is a value it carries, not part of its type, so the compiler cannot rely on it.

choices.text: It compiles and panics if `s` has fewer than three elements
choices.why: Nothing is deferred to run time here; the call never compiles.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: a `[]int` and a `[3]int` are different types
choices.why: Right. The lab said `cannot use s (variable of type []int) as [3]int value in argument to sum`.

choices.text: It compiles, and the function receives the slice's three words
choices.why: A slice's three words are what a `[]int` parameter would receive; this parameter wants an array.

prompt: `a` is a `[5]int` and `s := a[1:3]`. What are `len(s)` and `cap(s)`?
hint: The capacity runs to the end of the array.

choices.text: 3 and 5
choices.why: 3 counts index 3 as included, and 5 is the array's length, not the slice's capacity.

choices.text: 2 and 2
choices.why: The capacity does not stop at the length; the array goes on past index 2.

choices.text: 2 and 4
choices.why: Right. Indices 1 and 2 make the length; from index 1 to the end of the array is 4.

choices.text: 2 and 5
choices.why: The capacity counts from where the slice starts, index 1, not from the array's start.

prompt: `a` is a `[8]int` and `s := a[2:5]`. What is `cap(s)`?
hint: From where `s` starts to the end of `a`.

prompt: `a := [5]int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}` and `s := a[1:3]`. After `s[0] = 99`, what does `fmt.Println(a)` print?
hint: Was anything copied when `s` was made?

choices.text: `[10 20 30 40 50]`, because `s` is a copy of two elements
choices.why: Slicing copies no elements; `s` points into `a`.
That takes `s[0]` for the array's first element, but `s` starts at index 1 of `a`.
Right. `s[0]` and `a[1]` are the same element, and `&s[0] == &a[1]` printed `true`.

choices.text: A compile error, since a slice of an array is read-only
choices.why: Slices of arrays are as writable as the array; the assignment compiled and ran.

prompt: With `s := a[1:3]` and `t := a[2:5]` over the same array, which pair of expressions names one element?
hint: Work out which index of `a` each one is.

choices.why: `s[0]` is `a[1]` and `t[0]` is `a[2]`: two different elements.
Right. Both are `a[2]`, which is why writing 77 through `t` changed what `s` printed.
`t[1]` is `a[3]`, one past `s[1]`.

choices.text: None, because each slice gets its own copy of the elements it shows
choices.why: Slicing copies nothing; both slices look into `a`.

prompt: What does a slice value itself hold?
hint: The figure drew it.

choices.text: Its elements, in an array that grows when it fills up
choices.why: That is the "dynamic array" picture. The elements live in an array the slice points into.

choices.text: A copy of the elements between its two indices
choices.why: Nothing is copied when a slice is made; `s[0] = 99` changed the array.

choices.text: A pointer into an array, a length and a capacity, and no elements
choices.why: Right. Three words, and no elements of its own.

choices.text: The array's name and the two indices it was sliced with
choices.why: A slice literal's array has no name at all; the slice holds a pointer, not a name.

prompt: `a` is a `[5]int` and `s := a[1:3]`. Match each expression to what the lab printed for it.
hint: One of them comes from section 03.

prompt: You need to know whether two `[]int` hold the same numbers in the same order. What do you write?
hint: `==` was refused for slices.

choices.why: Refused: `slice can only be compared to nil`.
That asks whether both start at the same element of one array, which two equal slices need not do.

choices.text: `slices.Equal(s, u)`
choices.why: Right. It compares the lengths, then the elements in order.

choices.text: `len(s) == len(u) && cap(s) == cap(u)`
choices.why: Equal lengths and capacities say nothing about the numbers inside.

prompt: `addFour(s []int)` runs `s = append(s, 4)`. After `addFour(nums)`, with `nums` holding three elements, what is `len(nums)`?
hint: Whose `s` did the assignment change?

choices.text: 4, because `append` added to the array `nums` uses
choices.why: Even when the array has room, the caller's length is in the caller's slice, which nothing changed.

choices.text: 3, the length it had before the call
choices.why: Right. The function assigned to its own copy; the caller's slice still says length 3.

choices.text: 4, because slices are passed by reference
choices.why: A slice is passed as a copy of three words; lesson 22 takes that picture apart.

choices.text: 0, since `append` empties the slice it is handed
choices.why: `append` never removes anything; inside, `s` had four elements.

prompt: `setFirst(s []int)` runs `s[0] = 100`. What does the caller's `nums`, `[1 2 3]` before the call, hold afterwards?
hint: Where does the copy's pointer lead?

choices.text: `[1 2 3]`, because the function received a copy
choices.why: It did, but a copy of three words, and the pointer in it leads to the caller's array.

choices.text: `[100 2 3]`, because the write went through to the shared array
choices.why: Right. The copy's pointer leads to the caller's array, and the element was written there.
Assigning to `s[0]` replaces an element; it does not insert one.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses writing to a parameter's elements
choices.why: It compiled, ran and printed `[100 2 3]`.

prompt: To add 4 to the end of `nums` and keep the result, write `nums = ___(nums, 4)`.
hint: A built-in function; the compiler refuses a call to it that throws the result away.

prompt: On the lab's amd64 machine an `int` is 8 bytes. How many bytes does `unsafe.Sizeof` report for a `[500]int`?
`func reset(s []int) { s = []int{} }` is called as `reset(nums)`, with `nums` holding `[1 2 3]`. What does `nums` hold afterwards?
hint: The assignment is to the parameter itself, not to an element.

choices.text: `[1 2 3]`, as before the call
choices.why: Right. Assigning a new slice to `s` changes the function's copy and nothing the caller holds.

choices.text: `[]`, because the caller's slice now points at an empty array
choices.why: Only the copy points there. The caller's three words were never written.
That would need the elements reset to zero, and none was written; `setFirst` changed one by indexing, and `reset` never indexes.

choices.text: A compile error: `s` is assigned and never used
choices.why: Parameters are exempt from that rule; the lab compiled it and `nums` printed `[1 2 3]`.

prompt: Order these by how many bytes a function call copies to pass one, most first, on the lab's amd64 machine.
hint: An array is copied whole; a slice is three words whatever it shows.

prompt: `func withFour(s []int) []int { return append(s, 4) }`. A colleague writes `withFour(nums)` on a line of its own, with no assignment. What happens?
hint: The compiler's refusal was for one particular function.

choices.text: It is refused as `is not used`, like a bare `append` call
choices.why: That check is for built-ins like `append`. Your own function's result may be thrown away, and the lab compiled it.

choices.text: It compiles, and `nums` keeps its old length
choices.why: Right. The longer slice was returned to nobody, which is the bug returning the slice was meant to prevent.

choices.text: It compiles, and `nums` gains the 4 because `append` ran on it
choices.why: `append` ran on the function's copy; the caller's length changes only if the caller stores the result.

choices.text: It panics at run time, because the returned slice was not stored
choices.why: Nothing checks that at run time; the program ran and printed `[1 2 3] 3`.
